title: In-house legal is approaching an inflection point
summary: Our engineering output tripled in three months once enough of the right pieces were in place. In-house legal work is heading for the same kind of step change.
body_markdown:
*Our engineering output tripled in three months once enough of the right pieces were in place. In-house legal work is heading for the same kind of step change.*


We're approaching an inflection point in how much legal work AI can complete on its own. I expect the result to be a step change in productivity: many legal tasks run autonomously and in-house teams get far more done with the people they have. For legal departments asked to support a growing business without growing headcount, that changes what the team can take on.


[Our introduction to this series](https://legora.com/blog/legal-work-without-limits) made the case that when legal work gets cheaper and faster, more of it becomes worth doing. This post covers the product thinking behind that.


I use coding as the analog throughout, because it's the one place where we see both sides: we build software ourselves, and we work with in-house legal teams every day.


## Our engineering team hit a tipping point this year


AI for coding has consistently run six to twelve months ahead of legal, and[in March](https://legora.com/blog/2026-the-year-of-agents-in-legal-ai) we wrote that legal was tracking the same curve as software development, one cycle behind.


Our own engineering team offers a glimpse of where legal is heading. For most of the past year, the amount each engineer shipped was improving at a slow and steady pace, even as the underlying models kept getting better. Then all of a sudden, between July and October the number of code changes we shipped to production more than tripled. In less than three months, we saw a dramatic increase in velocity that could not be attributed to increased headcount.


These productivity improvements tend to come gradually and then all of a sudden. Once enough of the right ingredients are in place a tipping point is reached and progress increases exponentially. For us, the final ingredient was our cloud agent setup. Once an agent running in the cloud could take a change all the way to production, our engineers could massively parallelize their work, running many agents at once instead of working on just one or a few things at a time.


## Legal work is approaching the same tipping point


I believe legal work is about to see the same kind of step change as software engineering. Right now we're in the gradual improvement stage, improving each of the individual ingredients. I expect it to keep looking like slow progress right up until it changes rapidly.


Three things had to be good enough before our engineering team reached its tipping point, and the same three have to be good enough in legal.


Ingredient


What tipped engineering


What it takes in legal


Models


Good enough to write the code


Good enough to do the legal reasoning


Tools


Cloud agents that take a change all the way to production


Building blocks that complete a workflow end to end


Setup


A clean, modular codebase with tests and automated checks


Your processes, playbooks and policies codified into the system


The models are improving every month as the labs race toward superintelligence. Building the tools that enable end-to-end legal work is our job at Legora. The third is up to each legal department: getting its own setup ready for agents, with help from the tools it uses.


## Legal work is made of a small set of building blocks


Let's start with the tools. Like most knowledge work, legal is composed of a discrete set of jobs to be done. Take a given legal task and break it down into the components needed to complete it. Do that across everything a legal department handles and you don't end up with hundreds of building blocks; you end up with maybe a few dozen, falling into roughly four categories:


-


**The agent.** Intelligence on tap. Agents are comprised of the model and the harness around it: the software that lets it plan, use tools and check its work.


-


**Data and context.** Whatever the task depends on: your contracts and policies, the law and regulation, and the systems your business runs on, from CRM to procurement.


-


**Instructions.** How your team wants the work done: your processes, playbooks, policies and escalation rules.


-


**Surfaces.** The places where the work gets done. Drafting needs a document editor, reviewing documents at scale needs a table, and work that moves between legal and the business needs task management.


Different legal tasks demand different combinations of largely the same building blocks. Take four areas of an in-house team's work: regulatory, contracts, M&A and litigation. This is roughly what each one needs.


Five of the twelve blocks are used by all four areas, and each area needs only one source of its own. That makes each new use case easier than the last. Swap the data as contracts workflow reads and you are most of the way to a regulatory one. Change who it is shared with as well and you have the start of one for an acquisition.


Because the building blocks are shared, each incremental improvement benefits every workflow that depends on it. This is what drives the step change. Conversely, the weakest block also becomes the limiting factor in the system: if one is missing or underpowered, the task stalls and comes back to a lawyer.


Take working with the rest of the business. Until we released Intake, an agent could draft an NDA or answer a policy question, but a lawyer still had to carry the request in from their inbox and the answer back out. Every workflow that starts with a colleague outside legal was waiting on that one block: sales contracts, routine policy questions, marketing and procurement approvals. Adding a single block can level up dozens of processes that all depend on it.


## Your team's setup has to be ready too


The third ingredient is your team's own setup: everything an agent needs in order to work the way your team does, written down and accessible. The models and the tools are the same for everyone who buys them. This part is yours, and I expect it to separate the legal departments that see a step change from the ones that see gradual gains from the same tools.


Engineering teams learned this first. Our CTO, Jake Lauritzen,[has argued](https://x.com/jacsebl/status/2122725653833244769) that an engineer's job is shifting from writing code to building the environment in which agents write good code: a clean, consistent codebase, conventions that are written down, and tests and automated checks so an agent can tell whether its change works. Lauren Tan, whose team at SpaceXAI reports shipping thousands of changes a month with coding agents,[says](https://ai.engineer/code/2026/talks/lauren-tan) the same. Her rule is that when an agent gets something wrong, the fix belongs in the system itself, as a constraint or an automated check, before it becomes another line of written instructions.


The same patterns hold in legal. The models are already as smart as most of the people they work alongside, if not smarter. What they don't know is what your team wants done and how it wants it done - you still have to explain both. For an in-house team, that comes down to three things:


-


**Get your documents in one place.** Many large enterprises have their contracts, playbooks and policies scattered across dozens of disparate systems.


-


**Write down how you want things to work.** The playbooks, negotiating positions, approval thresholds and escalation rules that live in senior lawyers' heads.


-


**Write down what good looks like.** The standard a piece of work has to meet, so the agent can check its own output before a lawyer sees it.


This also changes where legal judgment is applied. A decision about what is acceptable, written down once and enforced in AI systems, applies to every matter that follows. Lawyers are now responsible for handling the exceptions and making the hard calls.


All of this takes time from the people who know how your team works, but you don't have to do it alone. Skills and playbooks are how that knowledge gets captured in Legora, and our legal engineering team exists to help customers do exactly this. Much of the work will fall to legal operations, and my colleague Mark Allen covers how roles and teams change in[his piece in this series](https://legora.com/blog/legal-was-the-top-ai-user-in-the-company) .


## The next tipping point is review


Everything so far has been about reaching the first tipping point. But what happens next?


In software development, writing code is now effectively free, but that doesn't mean we produce infinite software. In any sufficiently complex system, the moment one constraint is eliminated, the bottleneck shifts to the next most constrained point in the system.


For us, that next point is code review. Simply put, agents write changes faster than people can read them. This bottleneck is harder to clear than the first, because it means trusting an agent to work on its own and ship changes that no human has reviewed line by line.


Nobody has fully solved this yet, but the approaches are converging. Lauren Tan[treats](https://ai.engineer/code/2026/talks/lauren-tan) human review as the most expensive check there is, to be spent only after automated checks have run and the agent has shown that its change works. Addy Osmani of Anthropic[argues](https://addyosmani.com/blog/agentic-code-review/) for matching review to risk. At Legora, we're building and iterating toward a world where agents ship code autonomously, while maintaining an extremely high bar for security, reliability and quality.


I expect clearing the code review bottleneck to result in the next tipping point.


Legal won't be far behind. If every contract, business request and piece of advice still needs the same lawyer attention, the lawyers become the bottleneck: at five times the output, review time per item has to fall by 80% just to keep the workload flat. Clearing it means the legal equivalent of an unreviewed code change: a contract markup that goes back to the business without a lawyer having read it.


I was a corporate lawyer before I moved into product, so I know how deeply "a lawyer reviews everything" is built into the way the profession manages risk. Letting work through without that review is obviously scary. Trust has to be earned, and the way to earn it is to narrow where a lawyer's review is required, one class of work at a time. Each class moves through three stages of review:


1.


**Review everything.** AI drafts and a lawyer checks every output.


2.


**Review exceptions.** The system handles routine cases and sends the unusual ones to a lawyer.


3.


**Work within delegated limits.** For defined classes of work, the system completes the task inside limits the legal team has set, and lawyers check samples and outcomes.


A class of work moves up only as far as the evidence supports: how the workflow performs against matters your lawyers have already reviewed, then the correction rate on samples once it's live. An NDA on your own paper might reach the third stage long before a negotiated customer agreement does, and some work should never leave the first. Accountability doesn't move, because the legal team still owns the limits.


You get there the way engineers do, with checks and guardrails built into the system around the model:


-


**Prevent errors by design.** Approved templates and clause options, so the agent is choosing among positions you have already accepted.


-


**Check for known failure modes.** Policy checks on every output: liability caps, governing law, the terms you never agree to.


-


**Verify independently.** A separate check of the result against the source documents and the authorities it relies on.


-


**Turn corrections into new checks.** When a lawyer catches a problem, it turns into a new check or guardrail, so it doesn't recur the next time.


A lawyer's correction then improves every future matter that uses the workflow. The analogy does have a limit: a bad code change can be reverted and a signed contract can't, so how reversible the output is should weigh heavily in what you delegate first.


## More capacity will not mean excess capacity


Suppose all of this gets solved and capacity explodes. You might expect excess capacity, but our view is that legal will see[a Jevons effect](https://legora.com/blog/legal-work-without-limits) , where making something cheaper increases how much of it gets used.


There are two reasons for this. As things get cheaper you want to do more of them, so work that wasn't economical before becomes worthwhile: reviewing every agreement where today you sample, or advising on a launch before anything is built. And the business itself is moving faster, because AI is doing the same thing to every other function. New business lines, more sales and new markets all generate additional legal work.


None of this arrives on its own. To start moving toward this reality, General Counsel and legal operations leaders need to be asking questions like:


-


Where does your team's time go today, and what makes that work slow?


-


Which processes live in which people's heads, and how will you get them written down?


-


What would it take for you to let an agent complete a piece of legal work without a lawyer reviewing it?


-


What would your team do with the capacity that frees up?


Our engineering team saw slow, steady progress for most of a year, and then output tripled in three months. The legal departments that work through these questions now are the ones that will be ready when the same thing happens to them.
